Damage to onion crop in Maharashtra 
*343     SHRI SANJAY RAUT:† 
SHRI TARIQ  ANWAR: 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether heavy rains and floods in Maharashtra have caused extensive 
damage to onion crop in Maharashtra, if so, the extent of loss and damage 
to the crop; 
(b) what percentage of demand for onion in the country is met by 
Maharashtra, and how far the recent onion crisis in the country was 
attributable to this damage; and 
(c) what Central aid, if any, was sought and given to the Government of 
Maharashtra to help the farmers out of the crisis caused by such damage 
to onion crop? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a) to 
(c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House.The question was actually 
asked on the floor of the House by Shri Sanjay Raut 
1 
 

RAJYA SABHA [16 December 2005] 
Statement 
(a) to (c) Heavy rains and floods in Maharashtra have caused extensive 
damage to onion crops during this year (2005). During April-May, 2005, 
unseasonal rain and high temperature during harevesting time of rabi crop 
resulted in poor quality which was responsible for reduced shelf-life because 
of which quantity of onion stored, decr eased by 25% in comparison to last 
year. Against 7 lakh tonnes stored in 2004, only 5.25 lakh tonnes could be 
stored in 2005. During July 2005, owing to continuous rains in Maharashtra, 
there was damage to the seed sown during early kharif, forcing the farmers to 
re-sow, causing production loss and delayed kharif crop in Maharashtra by 
about a month. Loss of nursery and delayed monsoon resulted in reduction of 
onion cropped area by about 15%. Again, during October, 2005, heavy rains 
damaged the kharif crop in some of the districts of Maharashtra. The overall 
loss in kharif production in Maharashtra is estimated to be about 43%. 
Against the production of 2.70 lakh tonnes in Khariff 2004, the production in 
Maharashtra during kharif, 2005 is 1.55 lakh tonnes. 
The State of Maharashtra meets 28% of  the total demand of onion in the 
country. As mentioned above, the unseasonal and excess rainfall is 
responsible for shortage in availability of onion and consequent price hike. 
This situation prevailed for a short period during the month of October 2005, 
which soon stabilized due to sufficient arrival of onion from Rajasthan and 
other Southern States. 
Government of Maharashtra submitted a memorandum to the Central 
Government for the floods that occurred in July-August, 2005 indicating the 
total agricultural loss at Rs. 1239.57 crore. Memorandum of the State 
Government did not indicate crop-wise breakup of the losses. Government 
have approved release of an amount of Rs. 697.45 crore. 
SHRI SANJAY RAUT: Sir, the hon. Minister, in his reply, has agreed that 
heavy rains and floods have destroyed the onion crops in Maharashtra. 
Maharashtra is the highest producer of onion in the country. The onion bulbs 
should necessarily be stor ed in spacious and ventila ted structures, as they 
tend to spoil in cold-storages. Improper storage of onions makes them 
vulnerable to weather-related conditions. So, there is a need for creating more 
storage and allied facilities for onions, for which the Maharashtra 
Government needs the Central assistance. Is the

Co-ordination Committee for agricultural development 
*345. SHRIMATI VANGAGEETH A: Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have constituted the Agriculture Co-ordination 
Committee to focus on agricultural development and policy; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether Government have set any time-frame to implement the 
recommendations of such Committee; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a) to 
(d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (d) An Agriculture Coordination Committee has been recently 
constituted under the Chairmanship of the Prime Minister, to evolve a 
systematic approach to policy formulation on issues pertaining to agriculture 
and to promote inter-sectoral and inter-departmental coordination in planning 
and implementation. The Composition of the Committee is as follows: 
1. Prime Minister - Chairman 
2. Minister for Agriculture and Food & Civil Supplies & Consumer 
Affairs 
3. Minister of Chemicals and Fertilizers 
4. Minister of Finance 
5. Minister for Commerce & Industry 
6. Minister for Water Resources

8. Minister of Panchayati Raj 
9. Minister of State for Food Processing 
10. Minister of State for Science & Technology 
11. Deputy Chairman, Planning Commission  
12. Chairman, Economic Advisory Council 
13. Chairman, National Commission on Farmers 
 
14. Member (Agriculture), Planning Commission 
15. Principal Secretary to PM Convenor 
Secretaries of the Ministries/Departm ents concerned would be permanent 
invitees. The Chairman could invite any Minister/Officer depending upon the 
context. 
The Committee may commission specialized studies depending upon the 
requirements, which arise from time to time and could engage in the 
following tasks:— 
(a) Identify key areas that require fresh  policy initiatives, particularly 
those of an inter-sectoral nature. 
(b) Outline the follow-up action that needs to be taken to implement 
identified policy initiatives. 
(c) Identify institutional mechanisms to implement policies and 
programmes. 
(d) Monitor key policy initiatives. 
(e) To oversee and coordinate the in tegrated implementation of those 
recommendations of the National Commission on Farmers that are 
accepted by the Government. 
The Committee has not yet given its recommendations.

Price control on drugs 
*346. SHRI V. NARAYANASAMY: W ill the Minister of CHEMICALS 
AND FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are planning to ease control on pricing of drugs 
manufactured in India; and 
(b) whether Government studied the position that would arise by relaxing 
the control on drugs prices after which the drugs will become costlier for the 
consumers? 
THE MINISTER OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI RAM 
VILAS PASWAN): (a) and (b) A Statem ent is laid on the Table of the 
House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) As per the present Pharma Pricing Policy, the 74 bulk drugs 
specified in the First Schedule of th e Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 1995 
(DPCO, 95) and the formulations based thereon are under price control and 
their prices are fixed/revised by the National Pharmaceutical Pricing 
Authority (NPPA) in accordance with the provisions of the DPCO, 95. 
Prices of non-Scheduled formulations are fixed by the manufacturers 
themselves keeping in view the vari ous factors like cost of production, 
marketing/selling expenses, R&D expenses, trade commission, market 
competition, product innovation, product  quality etc. The NPPA monitors 
the prices of medicines as per monthly Retail Audit Reports of ORG-IMS 
Research Pvt. Ltd. The Government takes corrective measures where the 
public interest is found to be adversely affected. 
The Government announced the 'Pharmaceutical Policy 2002' in February 
2002. However, a public interest litigation filed in the High Court of 
Karnataka at Bangalore resulted in an Order dated 12.11.2002 from Hon'ble 
High Court, which stopped the Government from implementing the price 
control regime envisaged in the Pharmaceutical Policy 2002. This 
Department filed a Special Leave Petition (SLP) before the Supreme Court 
of India against the Order of the Ka rnataka High Court, which has been 
admitted as SLP (C) No. 3668/2003. The Supreme Court vide its order dated 
10.3.2003 directed the Government, inter-alia, that, "we suspend the 
operation of the order to the extent it directs that the Policy dated 15.2.2002 
shall not be implemented. However we direct that the petitioner 
9 

RAJYA SABHA [16 December, 2005] 
shall consider and formulate appropri ate criteria for ensuring essential and 
life saving drugs not to fill out of the price control and further directed to 
review drugs, Which are essential a nd lite saving in nature till 2nd May, 
2003". ministry of Health and Family Welfare has brought out the National 
List of Essential Medicines, 2003 after the review of the National Essential 
Drugs List, 1996. The matter is sub-judice before the Supreme Court. 
The National Common Minimum Programme as adopted by the 
Government aims, inter-alia, to ensure availability of life saving drugs at 
reasonable prices. In the light of National Common Minimum Programme 
and the observations of the Supreme Court in SLP (C) No. 3668/2003, the 
Government constituted a Committee under the Chairmanship of Joint 
Secretary (PI) to suggest measures fo r fulfilling the objectives of National 
Common Minimum Programme to ensure the availability of life saving drugs 
at reasonable prices. This Committee has submitted its interim report to the 
Government. 
Subsequently, a Task Force under the Chairmanship of Dr. Pronab Sen, 
Principal Adviser, Planning Commission was constituted to explore options 
other than price control to make available life saving drugs at reasonable 
prices. During its meetings, the Task Fo rce deliberated upon almost all the 
recommendations made in its interim Report by the Committee under the 
Chairmanship of Joint Secr etary. The Task Force has submitted its report to 
the Government on the 20th September, 2005. Some of the salient 
recommendations of Task Force regarding the price management are, that 
Price Controls should be imposed on the 'essentiality' of the drug and not on 
the basis of turnover and its should be applied only to formulations and not to 
bulk drugs to promote generic drugs, to establish price negotiation process 
for new patented drugs, to streamline the bulk procurement regime, to 
exempt the excise duty, customs duty and other levies on cancer and anti 
HIV/AIDS drugs, to reduce the excise duty on drugs from 16 to 8%, to 
enhance the exemption limit of SSI units from Rs. 1 Crores to Rs. 5 Crores 
etc. 
A Core Group under the Chairmanship  of Joint Secretary (PI) has been 
constituted by this Department to examine the recommendations of the Task 
Force and to draft a new Pharmaceutical Policy. The Government is also in 
consultation with various stakeholders is examining the raoornmendations of 
the Task Force. Based on this a new Pharmaceutical Policy 
10

Is likely to be announced shortly. The main objective of the 
pharmaceutical policy will be to ensure availability of the life saving drugs 
and essential drugs at reasonable prices.

Statement 
The salient features of the National Steel Policy 
• The NSP sets out a broad roadmap for the Indian Steel Industry in its 
journey towards reform, restructing adn globalization. 
• The long-term goal of the NSP is that India should have a modern and 
efficient steel industry of world standards, catering to diversified steel 
damand. The focus of the policy is to achieve global competitiveness 
not only in terms of cost, quality and product-mix but also in terms of 
global benchmarks of efficiency and productivity. This will require 
indegenous production of 110 million tonnes per annum by 2019-20 
from the 2004-05 level of 38 million tonnes. This implies a 
compounded annual growth of 7.3 percent per annum. 
• In order to achieve the goal of 110 million tonnes of steel production 
by 2019-20, the country would require 190 million tonnes of iron ore 
and 70 million tonnes of coking coal. The NSP seeks to remove the 
supply-side constraints to the growth of this industry in an open, 
globally integrated and competitive enviornment. 
• The NSP seeks adopt a multi-pronged strategy to move towards the 
long-term policy goal. On the demand side, the strategy would be to 
create incremental demand through promotional efforts, creation of 
awareness and strengthening the deliv ery chain, particularly in rural 
areas. On the supply side, the strategy would be to facilitate 
17 

RAJYA SABHA [16 December, 2005] 
creation of additional capacity, remove procedural and policy 
bottlenecks in the availability of inputs such as iron ore and coal, make 
higher investments in R&D an d encourage the creation of 
infrastructure such as roads, railways, and ports. 
• The NSP targets a per capita consumption level of about 165kg. In 
urban areas and 4kg. in rural areas by 2019-20 as compared to 77kg. 
and 2 kg., respectively in 2004-05. The industry will be encouraged to 
set up new block level rural stock points in order to boost steel 
consumption. Measures will be taken to incorporate steel structures in 
the CPWD code for goverment buildin gs and to include steel usage in 
the curricula for technical institutes. 
• In order to achieve the strategic goal of 110 million tonnes of steel 
production by 2019-20, the industry would need additional capital Rs. 
2,30,000 crores. In addition, funds would be required for technological 
upgrade of existing facilities. 
• in order to mobilize such vast resources NSP seeks to encourage 
foreign direct investment. In addition the policy also seeks to devise 
suitable fiscal incentives for the steel industry. 
• The NSP seeks to support development of risk-hedging instruments 
like futures and derivatives to contain price volatility in the steel 
market. 
• The NSP seeks to strengthen the existing training and research 
facilities available to the domestic steel industry so as to provide 
suitable training programmes especi ally for the secondry small-scale 
units and also to collect and analy ze data on important parameters of 
the industry. 
• The NSP seeks to mount aggressive R&D efforts to create 
manufacturing capability for special types of steel, substitute coking 
coal, use iron ore fines, develop new products suited to rural needs, 
enhance material and energy efficiency, utilize waste, and arrest 
environmental degradation. 
• The NSP acknowledges the important role played by the secondary 
steel sector in providing employment, meeting local demand of steel in 
rural and semi-urban areas, and meeting thecountry's demand of some 
special products and seeks to endeavour to provide the 
18 

[16 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
necessary feedstock to these units at reasonable prices from major 
plants through the existing mechan ism of State Small Industries 
Corporations. 
  The NSP recognizes the fact that  integration of the Indian steel 
industry with the global economy requires that the industry should be 
protected from unfair trade practices, which become common 
especially during periods of downturn. The NSP therefore, envisages 
institution of mechanisms for important surveillance, and monitoring 
export subsidies in other countries.

Health care for ail 
*344. SHRI C. PERUMAL: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether any target for taking health care to all parts of the country has 
been fixed; 
33 

RAJYA SABHA [16 December, 2005] 
(b) if so , the details thereof; and 
(c) whether Government are aware th at CN's health committee and 
Escorts Heart Institute have conducted a study and found that Rs 1 lakh cores 
will be required for 'Health-care for All project? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRYOF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKALAKSHMI): (a) and (b) 
The National Health Policy, 2002, laid down the main objective as achieving 
an acceptable standard of good health  amongst the general population of the 
country. This was targeted to be achieved by establishing new infrastructure 
in deficient area and by upgrading infrastructure in the existing institutions. 
Taking into account the gap in health  care facilities, National Health Policy, 
2002, envisages an increase in health s ector expenditure to 6% GDP with 2% 
of GDP being contributed as public health investment by the year 2010. 
The National Common Minimum Programme of the Government has also 
focused attention on increasing public investment in health. It is proposed to 
increase the expenditure in the health sector to the level of 2-3% of the GDP 
by increased contributions from the Central and State Governments. 
Towards this end, the Government has launched a National Rural Health 
Mission, which seeks to provide effect ive health care to rural population 
throughout the country with special focus on 18 States with poor health 
indicators and weak health infrastructure. The main objective is to provide 
accessible, affordable, accountable, ef fective and reliable health care, 
especially to poor and vulnerable sections of population with the ultimate 
objective to achieve Population Stabili zation Programme in the high fertility 
states of the country. Under the strategy of NRHM, the gap in the existing 
scenario of rural health care is to be addressed th rough 2.5 lakh Accredited 
Social Health Activists (ASHA) to assist the Anganwadi Worker and ANM at 
village level to make the increased h ealth services accessible to the rural 
people of the country. It is also proposed to upgrade CHCs to the level of 
India Public Health Standards (IPHS). NRHM has been launched for a period 
of 7 years (2005-2012) i.e. for two years of Tenth Plan and full Eleventh 
Plan.

(c) The Cll National Committee on Health Care commissioned Mckinsey 
and Company for a Study in the year 2002, to define an achievable way 
forward for health care. The stud y has concluded that changing 
demographics, diseases profile and rising treatment costs will cause spending 
on health care to more than double by 2012. To meet this  increase in the 
demand for health care, improvement in infrastructure will require 
investments in hospitals, medical colleges, nursing schools and hospital 
management schools of Rs. 100,000 Crores to Rs. 140,000 crores over the 
next 10 years.

Decline in fish production 
*358. SHRI PRAMOD MAHAJAN:  Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether there has been a great fall in  fish production especially wild 
stock from sea and rivers; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(c) the corrective measures being unde rtaken to stimulate the fish 
production? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a) 
Though the overall fish production from the country has been on the 
increase, marine fish production has been more or less steady at 28-29 lakh 
tonnes during 2000-2004 and has shown a slight fall to 27.8 lakh tonnes 
during 2004-05. There has been some fluctuation in riverine capture fisheries 
in the recent years. 
(b) The decline in marine fish production during 2004-05 is mainly 
attributed to the major havoc cause d by tsunami during December, 2004. 
Topographic changes due to construction of dams, bridges and barrages and 
increased land based pollution besides intensive fishing are the major reasons 
for decline in riverine capture fisheries. 
(c) In the marine sector resource conservation through closed seasons, 
mesh regulations and such other management measures are being 
implemented for replenishing the fish stock. Apart from this, production 
from the deep sea is being augmented by encouraging investment in the 
Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ). Measur es to decongest the coastal waters 
by encouraging fishing beyond territorial waters by enabling the existing 
class of mechanised boats and encouraging introduction of the intermediate 
craft are being implemented. River ranching, abating pollution and fishing 
regulations are being practiced to enhance the health of riverine fish stock. 
Thrust is being given to increase fish production through aquaculture besides 
assisting the sector through various Central and Centrally Sponsored 
Schemes to improve fish production.

AGRICULTURE be pleased to state:

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI KANTI LAL BHURIA): (a) According to the 59th Round of National 
Sample Survey conducted during the period January-December 2003, the 
total number of persons dependent on agriculture was 492.2 million. This 
constitutes 66% of the total rural population.

forestry, logging and fishing to Gross Domestic Products (GDP) at 1993-94 
prices along with annual growth rates during last ten years are given in the

not fixed. However, average annual growth rate targets for the Five-Year 
Plans are fixed by the Planning Commission.

steadily declining as compared to other sectors. The details of percentage

†2588. SHRI SURENDRA LATH: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the farmers of the country have requested Government to 
consider Gram Panchayat as unit inst ead of Block under crop insurance 
scheme so that farmers could get insurance on damage of crops in entire 
Panchayat, due to natural calamity; 
(b) if so, the steps taken by Government in this regard and the outcome 
thereof; and 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
72 

[16 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI KANTI LAL BHURIA). (a) to (c) Yes, Sir. Farmers and 
Implementing States have requested from time to time to reduce the unit area 
of insurance to Village or Gram Panchayat level so as to make more realistic 
assessment of crop loss and compen sation under National Agricultural 
Insurance Scheme (NAIS).

improvements required in the existing crop insurance schemes has examined

regarding implementation of the recommendations of the Group. 
National Horticulture Mission 
2589. SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA. Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE 
be pleased to state: 
(a)the aims and objectives of the National Horticulture Mission; 
(b)the details of areas that have been  identified in Andhra Pradesh which 
are regionally different from others  for cluster approach and for the 
development of horticulture crops in the State; 
(c) the difference between Technology Mission for integrated 
development to Horticulture and NHM;

Pradesh;and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI KANTI LAL BHURIA): (a) The main objectives of the National 
Horticulture Mission (NHM) are: 
(i) To provide holistic growth of the horticulture sector through an area 
based regionally differentiated strategies which include research, 
technology promotion, extension, post harvest management, 
73 

RAJYA SABHA [16 December, 2005] 
processing and marketing, in consonance with comparative advantage 
or each State/region and its diverse agro-climatic features; 
(ii) To enhance horticulture produc tion, improve nutritional security and 
income support to farm households; 
(iii) To establish convergence and synergy among multiple on-going and 
planned programmes for horticulture development; 
(iv) To promote, develop and disseminate technologies, through a seamless 
blend of traditional wisdom and modem scientific knowledge; 
(v) To create opportunities for employment generation for skilled and 
unskilled persons, especially unemployed youth. 
(b) Total 12 districts namely, Srikakulam, West Godavari, Guntur, 
Ananthapur, Prakasham, Cuddapah, Kurnool, Mahabubnagar, Rangareddy, 
Nalgonda, Khammam and Nizamabad have been identified in the State of 
Andhra Pradesh with cluste r approach for nine horticultural crops based on 
their respective production strength and potential for further development. 
(c) Under the Centrally Sponsored Scheme on Technology Mission of 
Integrated Development of Horticultu re, there are four mini missions (i) 
Research, (ii) Production, (iii) Post Harvest Management & Marketing and 
(iv) Processing, Whereas, under NHM there is no such compartmentalization 
of mini missions. Besides, activities of research and processing are to be 
funded by the respective Departments. Technology Mission is being

Foodgrain production and shortage 
†2592. SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA: 
SHRI MOTILAL VORA: 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) the ratio of growth rate of foodgrain production and population in the 
country; 
(b) the extent of shortfall registered in the foodgrain stocks in the country 
during the last two years; 
(c) whether Government have taken any concrete steps to avoid import of 
foodgrains from foreign countries; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI KANTI LAL BHURIA) (a) The average growth rate of foodgrain 
production during the period 2000-01 to 2004-05 is 2.06% while the 
projected average growth rate of population during the period 2001 to 2005 is 
1.60%. Thus, the rate of growth of foodgrain production is about 25% higher 
than that of population. 
(b) The stock of rice and wheat as on 1st July 2004 was 29.92 million 
tonnes against the buffer norm of 24.30 million tonnes. The stock of rice and 
wheat as on 1st July 2005 was 24.53 million tonnes against the new buffer 
norm of 26.90 million tonnes. 
(c) and (d) India is a net exporter of rice and wheat but it imports pulses to 
meet the demand and supply gap. For increasing the production of 
foodgrains, schemes like Integrated Crop Development Programme (ICDP) 
for Wheat, Rice, Coarse Cereals and Inte grated Scheme of Oilseeds, Pulses, 
Oil Palm and Maize (ISPOM) are being implemented in various states of the 
country. To increase the irrigated areas, micro irrigation systems are 
promoted apart from providing financial support to complete the last mile 
projects through accelerated irrigation benefit programme.

Farmers leaving agriculture 
2596.   SHRI SANJAY RAUT: 
SHRI R.K. ANAND: 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that more than 40 per cent farmers would like to 
quit agriculture business due to unsafe and low margin to agro-produce, 
water dependent production as well as unavailability of agriculture loan on 
lower percentage of interest rate in the country; 
(b) if so, Government's views and reaction thereto; and 
(c) the details of measures taken or proposed to be taken for improving 
the current unfavourable atmosphere in the agriculture by keeping in view 
the poor farmers of the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI KANTILAL BHURIA) (a) As per the 59th Round Survey Report of 
National Sample Survey Organisation submitted in July, 2005,40 per cent of 
the farmer households to not like farming as a profession as they consider it 
unprofitable, risky, lacking social status  etc. While 27 per cent of the farmer 
households consider agriculture being not profitable, 8 per cent consider it as 
a risky venture. Remaining 5 per cent dislike it for some other reasons, which 
also include lack of social status. 
(b) and (c) The Government is seized of the problems being faced by the 
farmers. A number of measures have been taken by the Government to 
increase production and productivity in agriculture sector as also to raise the 
farm income by ensuring remunerative prices and thereby reasonable return 
to them. The measures, inter-alia, include easy and timely availability of 
institutional credit in a hassle free manner to the farmer at low rate of interest 
better risk management through implementation of crop insurance 
80

scheme, strengthening of marketing and storage facilities, promotion of 
agricultural diversification towards income enhancing crops and activities 
suitable to small holdings, sustainable dry-land farming, subsidy and price 
support measures like announcement of Minimum Support Prices and 
organizing of purchase operations to prevent distress sales by the farmers. 
A number of specific Schemes are be ing implemented for the benefit of 
farmers including small and marginal farmers. Prominent among these are 
National Horticulture Mission, Macro Management of Agricultural Scheme, 
Integrated Scheme of Oilseeds, Pu lses, Oil Palm and Maize (ISOPOM), 
Technology Mission on Cotton, Technology Mission on Coconut. 
Technology Mission for Integrated Development of Horticulture in North 
Eastern States including Sikkim, Ja mmu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh 
and Uttaranchal, Seed Village Scheme, Strengthening of Agricultural

provided to the farmers. Besides, effo rts are also on to cover larger areas 
under irrigation to reduce dependence on rain.

(SHRI KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) to (d) The use of quality inputs like seeds,

production and productivity. Accordingly,  cultivars, pesticides and fertilizers

Problem in agriculture sector 
†  2602. SHRI RAM JETHMALANI: 
SHRI RAJ MOHINDER SINGH MAJITHA: 
. Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have conducted a survey with regard to the 
problems being faced in the development of agriculture sector; 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
96 

[16 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) if so, the main problems identified so far; 
(c) the problems out of the above which are due to paucity of funds; 
(d) the problems which are due to lack of knowledge; and 
(e) the decline noticed in agriculture sector due to the same? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) to (d) The National Sample Survey 
Organisation (NSSO), Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation 
conducted the Situation Assessment Survey of Farmers in 2003 covering 
different aspects like educational level of farmer households, level of living 
as measured by consumer expenditure and indebtedness, their farming 
practices and preferences, resource availability and their awarness of 
technological developments and access to modern technology. The areas of 
concern as found in the survey reports include high indebtedness of the 
farmer households, consumption level below the average of rural households, 
less accessibility to modern technology, poor awareness on certain important 
schemes like Minimum Support Pri ce and Crop Insurance and less 
participation in group activities through cooperative societies etc. 
(e) In India, agricultural growth is largely influenced by rainfall and 
climatic conditions since about 60 per cent area is still rain fed. The latest 
statistics released by Central Statistical Organisation shows that agricultural 
sector grew by 1.1 per cent during 2004-05 and the estimated average growth 
rate during the first two quarters of the current year i.e. 2005-06 is 2 per cent. 
Cotton production 
2603. SHRI PYARELAL  KHANDELWAL Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that over 230 lakh bales of cotton was produced in 
the cotton season 2004-05; 
(b) whether the cotton crop is expected to be over 270 lakh bales in the 
cotton season 2005-06 and whether this will affect the prices; 
(c) whether Government are contemplating to export surplus cotton; 
97 

RAJYA SABHA [16 December, 2005] 
(d) whether Government are aware that China will be short of cottion by 
almost 2.5 to 3 million metric tonnes in the cotton season 2005-06; and 
(e) the details of the cotton export plan? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) and (b) The Cotton Advisory Board had 
placed the level of cotton production du ring cotton season  2004-05 at 243 
lakh bales (of 170 Kg. each). The estimated level of cotton production for the 
cotton season 2005-06 is around 250 lakh bales. However, the final 
estimation of cotton production for the cotton season 2005-06 is yet to be 
made. 
With good prospects of cotton crop for the second consecutive season as 
also due to easy availability of cotton, the domestic prices during 2005-06 
season have been subdued. As per the information supplied by the Cotton 
Corporation of India (CCI), the pr ogressive average rate of kapas was 
varying between Rs. 1723/- per quintal and Rs. 1977/- per quintal in different 
States for various varieties as on 12th December, 2005 against the Minimum 
Support Price (MSP) fixed by the Government at Rs. 1760/-and Rs. 1980/- 
per quintal for different staple lengths. 
(c) Exports of cotton in the country were placed under Open General 
Licence (OGL) from 2001 and anybody can export cotton from the country. 
However, looking to the carry over stock from previous year and the crop 
prospects, after meeting the domestic requirements, sufficient quantity may 
be available for exports during the current cotton season. Exports of cotton 
from the country shall however depend upon price parity. 
(d) As per the available reports, due to significant decrease in cotton area 
as also due to heavy rains in China (Main land), the cotton production is 
likely to be affected and as per In ternational Cotton Advisory Committee 
(ICAC) the same is estimated at 5.77 m illion tonnes as against 6.32 million 
tonnes during the previous year. As against this, significantly higher textile 
exports and expanding domestic textile consumption is expected to boost 
cotton use in China (Main land) from 8.2 to 8.6 million tonnes. As per latest 
ICAC release of 1st November, 2005, with projected gap of 2.86 million 
tonnes between production and consumption and with low carry over stocks, 
China (main land) is expected to increase its imports to fill the gap. The 
imports by China are forecast at 2.93 million tonnes as against 1.39 million 
tonnes last season. 
98 

[16 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(e) As already stated above, the exports of cotton are under OGL.

NCF recommendation for grain banks 
2607. SHRI SITARAM YECHURY: Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the National Commission on Farmers has recommended for 
the creation of Grain Banks in the district where National Food for Work 
Programme is under implementation; 
(b) if so, the steps taken by Government in this regard; 
(c) what has been the impact of the creation of Grain Banks; and 
(d) if Government did not implemented it the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI KANTI LAL BHURIA): (a) The National Commission on Farmers 
has recommended setting up of 10,000 Community Grain Banks to cover all 
tribal villages including 150 districts identified for "National Food for Work 
Programme" having more than 50% population belonging to Scheduled 
Caste/Scheduled Tribe communities.

to Scheduled Castes/Scheduled Tribes  as also the Below Poverty Line/

hilly areas. During 2005-06, a sum of Rs. 20.20 Crores has been allocated

Agreement with manufacturers on drug price control 
2609. SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: W ill the Minister of CHEMICALS 
AND FERTILIZERS be pleased to state; 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have not been able to arrive at 
101 

RAJYA SABHA [16 December, 2005] 
an agreement with manufacturers to fix prices of life saving and other drugs; 
(b) if so, the areas of disagreement; and 
(c) what steps Government propose to take to ensure availability of life 
saving drugs to patients at reasonable rates? 
THE MINISTER OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI RAM 
VILAS PASWAN): (a) to (c) As per the present Pharma Pricing Policy, the 
74 bulk drugs specified in the First Schedule of the Drugs (Prices Control) 
Order, 1995 (DPCO, 95) and the formulations based thereon are under price 
control and their prices are fixed/re vised by the National Pharmaceutical 
Pricing Authority (NPPA) in accordance with the provisions ofthe DPCO,95. 
Prices of non-Scheduled formulations are fixed by the manufacturers 
themselves keeping in view the various factors like cost of production, 
marketing/selling expenses, R&D expenses, trade commission, market 
competition, product innovation, product quality etc., The NPPA monitors 
the prices of medicines as per monthly Retail Audit Reports of ORG-IMS 
Research Pvt. Ltd. The Government takes corrective measures where the 
public interest is found to be adversely affected. 
Subsequently, a Task Force under the Chairmanship of Dr. Pronab Sen, 
Principal Adviser, Planning Commission was constituted to explore options 
other than price control to make ava ilable life saving drugs at reasonable 
prices. During its meetings, the Task Force deliberated upon almost all the 
recommendations made in its interim Report by the Committee under the 
Chairmanship of Joint Secretary. The Ta sk Force has submitted its report to 
the Government on the 20th September, 2005. Some of the salient 
recommendations of Task Force regarding the price management are, that 
Price Controls should be imposed on the 'essentiality' of the drug and not on 
the basis of turnover and it should be applied only to formulations and not to 
bulk drugs, to promote generic drugs, to establish price negotiation process 
for new patented drugs, to streamline the bulk procurement regime, to exempt 
the excise duty, customs duty and other levies on cancer and anti-HIV/AIDS 
drugs, to reduce the excise duty on drugs from 16 to 8% , to enhance the 
exemption limit of SSI units from 
102 

[16 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Rs. 1 Crores to Rs. 5 Crores. All these recommendations would assist in 
ensuring that the essential medicines are available at reasonable prices. 
The Government in consultation with various stakeholders is examining 
the recommendations of the Task Force. Based on this a new Pharmaceutical 
Policy is likely to be announced shortly. However, there is no practice of 
having an agreement with manufacturers to fix the prices of life saving and 
other drugs.

the Government.

management etc.

Sulphur and Benzene contents in diesel and petrol. 
• Introduction of cleaner fuels like Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) and 
Liquified Petroleum Gas (LPG) in a few polluted cities. 
• Introduction of improved Pollution Under Control (PUC) certification 
system.

lodization of salt 
2650. SHRI THENNALA G. BA LAKRISHNA PILL AI: Will the 
Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the WHO has confirmed that even a modest dietary intake of 
iodine by people who are not iodine-deficient will not be harmful but 
beneficial; 
(b) whether Government will consider salt iodization as a public health 
measure and mandate for blanket iodination of salt at salt heads; and 
(c) whether Government have laid down proper packing norms for the 
manufacturers of iodised salt? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) 
According to World Health Organization document No. WHO/NHD/01.1, 
Iodine deficiency disorders are easiest and most cost effective of all disorders 
to prevent. The addition of  a small amount of Iodine to the salt that people 
consume every day is sufficient to prevent Iodine deficiency disorders. 
Consumption of Iodised salt (as per standards laid down under the 
Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954)by people who are not Iodine 
deficient is absolutely safe. 
(b) PFA Rules, 1955 have been amended vide GSR 670(E) dated 
17.11.2005 whereby restrictions have been imposed on the sale of common 
salt for direct human consumption unless the same is iodized. However, 
common salt would continue to be sold for iodization, iron fortification, 
animal use, preservation, manufacturing of medicines and industrial use with 
the prescribed label declaration. 
(c) Packing norms for iodized salt have not been prescribed under PFA 
Rules, 1955. However, as per practice the iodized salt is packed for retail sale 
in polythene packages and for bulk transporation it is packed in bags. The 
iodized salt is not transported in loose conditions. 
To take care of loss of iodine during storage and transportation of iodized 
salt the parameter of iodine content in iodized salt has been prescribed both 
at manufacturer's level at not less than 30 ppm and at retail level at not less 
than 15 ppm.

until early 1970s essentially showed prevalence rates of diabetes less than

According to data from the Sample Registration System (SRS) of the 
office of the Registrar General of India (RGI) the Maternal Mortality Ratio 
(MMR) in India was estimated as 407 per 100,000 live births in 1998. 
Subsequent estimates are not available. Based on this data, it is estimated 
that more than 1.1 lakh women die in India every year due to causes related

According to the data from SRS of RGI for Infant Mortality Rate (IMR)

the first year of life (Infant Mortality Rate). Of these deaths, 
27 occur during the first week of life and another 13 occur within the first

during the rest of the 11 months of first year of life. As per the SRS data 
released by RGI for the year 2002, 17.8 children out of all the children below 
5 years die every year. All the indicat ors have been showing a declining 
trend over the years.

complication of pregnancy through Panchayat, provision of drugs and 
equipments at First Referral Units (FRUs), provision of contractual staff like

anesthetists. In the second  phase of theRCH Programme, provision has been

life (Infant Mortality Rate). Of these deaths, 27 occur during the first week 
of life and another 13 occur within the first 28 days of life. Thus it is not 
correct to say that 50% children born in the country die within first three-
four weeks after birth. 
Essential New born care and management of children with illnesses 
during the first 28 days of life has been included as a focused intervention 
under the RCH Programme for achieving reduction in deaths during the first 
28 days of life. Under this, the health workers and families are being trained 
to provide essential care to the new boms which includes keeping the child 
warm, initiation of breastfeeding immediately after birth and prevention of 
infections. 
Besides this, under the Reproductive and Child Health Programme (RCH) 
being implemented in all States of the country various other interventions for 
reduction of infant mortality rate are being implemented. These include 
immunization against fixed vaccine communicable diseases, control of death 
during diarrhea, control of deaths due to acute respiratory infections; 
prophylaxis against vitamin A defici ency and iron deficiency anaemia, 
essential new born care and promotion of exclusive breastfeeding and 
appropriate complementary feeding practices.

Regulation of Clinical Research 
2672.    DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
DR. KARAN SINGH: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether international scientific journals recently raised doubts on 
credibility of certain drug research work in India; 
(b) whether his Ministry is taking steps to regulate clinical research. 
(c) if so, whether Government have set up a Central Drug Standard 
Control Organisation under Drug Controller General of India for the 
purpose: 
(d) whether Government have contacted a panel of regulators mostly 
eminent doctors and researchers to inspect  the research sites in their zones; 
and 
(e) if so, to what extent these steps will be helpful to regulate clinical 
research? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (e) 
Certain country specific issues such as  lack of clear regulatory norms and 
intellectual property right issues were earlier considered barriers to global 
clinical research development in India. Now, regulations for conducting 
clinical trials in the country have be en prescribed under Rules-122DA-122E 
& Schedule-Y to the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945. 
Good Clinical Practices (GCP), an et hical and scientific quality standard 
for designing and conducting and recording trials data etc. has been 
published in 2001. Ethical guidelines for conducting human trials have also 
been published by Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) in 2000. 
In the past clinical trials in India, pertaining to totally new molecules have 
been very miniscule. However, this trend is now changing and the numbers 
of multicentric global clinical trials in India is expected to increase. 
171 

RAJYA SABHA [16 December, 2005] 
CDSCO has, therefore evolved a strategy to start inspections of clinical trial 
centers. 
Number of workshops have already been held in coordination with 
Department of Pharmacology, BYL Nair Hospital, Mumbai along with 
centers at AIIMS, New Delhi, Pondicherry, Kolkata, Hyderabad to develop 
necessary Standard Operating Proceduresm (SOPs), protocols etc. A training 
programme for the prospective inspectors of clinical trials was conducted in 
New Delhi on 20-21 September 2005 with support from WHO and in 
partnership with various medical experts and researchers from pharma 
industry to develop competence and capacity to undertake inspections/ 
audits. 
These measures will significantly enhance standards of clinical trials and 
will address the prevailing perception about likely exploitation of Indian 
study subjects, especially the poor and illiterate.

Iron-ore export  
2731. SHRI B.K. HARIPRASAD: Will the Minister of STEEL be pleased to state: 
(a) whether India's iron ore production during 2004 was around 142 million tonnes 
against domestic demand of 56 million tonnes; 
(b) whether the R.K. Dang Committee has recommended that iron ore exports should 
be tapered off in a span of ten years from now; 
(c) whether steel industry is pitching for a total and immediate ban on iron ore 
exports, while the ore export lobby wants exports to continue indefinitely; and 
(d) whether an abrupt ban on iron ore export would adversely affect the ore mining 
industry in Karnataka and Goa with a lot of investments in ports and mines and the 
machinery would become idle? 
THE MINISTER OF STEEL (SHRI RAM VILAS PASWAN): (a) As per 
231 

RAJYA SABHA [16 December, 2005] 
provisional figures provided by Indian Bureau of Mines (IBM) the production 
of iron ore during 2004-05 was 142.7 million tonnes. IBM has not provided 
any firm estimate of domestic demand of iron ore during the same period. 
However, based on crude steel production during 2004-05, the domestic 
consumption of iron ore is estimated to be in excess of 54 million tonnes. 
(b) Exports of iron ore did not form a part of the terms of reference of the 
"Expert Group" which was constituted by the Ministry of Steel under the 
Chairmanship of Shri R.K. Dang as  hence no specific recommendation has 
been made in the report of the "Expert Group" for tapering off iron ore 
exports in a span of ten years from now. However, Shri R.K. Dang has 
separately submitted a list titled "Oth er observations and recommendations" 
covering areas outside the terms of re ference of the "Exp ert Group". This, 
inter alia, contains recommendations for stopping exports of high and 
medium grade lump iron ore (except if being sold under existing long term 
international contracts of NMDC); phasing out exports of high grade iron ore 
fines and canalization of exports, within ceilings, of medium grade iron ore 
fines. 
(c) Some steel producers and associations representing various sections of 
the steel industry have represented for placing curbs on export of iron ore. On 
the other hand, represented against any move for placing curbs or ban on 
exports of iron ore. 
(d) The iron ore produced in  Karnataka and Goa is predominantly medium 
and low grade. Besides production of fines is predominant in these states. The 
domestic and local demand for such ore is low, on account of inadequate 
agglomeration and benefication capacities in the country and limited local 
steel making capacities in these states. As such production in these states is 
primarily dependent on the export market and an abrupt ban on exports of iron 
ore can be expected to affect production of iron ore in these states. This could 
also have a consequential impact on utilization of investments in both ports 
and the mines.

PRIVATE MEMBER'S RESOLUTION Need to ameliorate economic 
condition of farmers in the backdrop of natural 
calamities 
SHRI V. NARAYANASAMY(Pondicherry):   Sir, I move the following 
Resolution- 
"Having regard to the fact that - 
(i) even after more than five decades of independence the overall lot of 
farmers, who constitute majority of  the population of the nation, has 
not improved to the desired level and it is indeed very sad that 
thousands of farmers have committed suicide during the last few 
years, unable to face the miseries and hardships by themselves and 
their families and due to the pressure on them to repay their loans 
taken from moneylenders, banks, cooperatives, etc.; 
(ii) majority of the farmers are inde bted in the country because they do 
not get remunerative prices of thei r produce mostly due to the faulty 
procurement policy of the Govern ment and the nexus between the 
private traders and the Governme nt procurement agencies which 
forces them to sell their produce at throwaway prices; 
(iii) the farmers face the brunt of natural calamities such as drought, flood 
and their crops, dwelling units, household items including food   
grains,   livestock    are   affected   and    their   miseries   are 
250 

[16 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
compounded     due    to   non   extension   of   compulsory   crop 
insurance to their crops and livestock; 
(iv) whenever the farmers grow bumper  crops the prices of the produces 
nosedive in the market and by the time Market Intervention is 
introduced all is over for the farmers; and 
(v)   Governments while formulating the Plans and incentives have not 
given adequate attention to the pl ight of farmers and that only a 
meagre  percentage of GDP has so far  been  allocated for the 
agriculture. 
this House urges upon the Government to - 
(a) announce a package for the farmers who are indebted or 
adversely affected, by natural calamity through waiver of loans, 
interest accrued on loans and by providing fresh loans to start 
agricultural operations and such other measures as the 
Government may deem necessary; 
(b) plug the loopholes in the procurement policy and give the 
minimum support price to the farmers without any hassles; 
(c) insure the farmers and their crops and livestock at a nominal 
premium or at   the Government   cost compulsorily; 
(d) allocate appropriate percentage of GDP to agriculture; 
(e) make Market    Intervention   compulsory   whenever   there    
is bumper  crop of any commodity; and 
(f) take such other measures for the welfare of farmers as the 
Government may deem necessary. 
Sir, this is a very important Resolution and aims at improving the 
life of our farmers in various fields, especially through adequate credit facilities 
for them, marketing support for their produce, strengthening  of cooperative 
institutions, enabling farmers to use the latest advancements of science and 
technology in the farm sector, insuring farmers produce, etc. These are the 
areas which I what the Government to consider seriously. 
Therefore, before going into the points one-by-one, I would like to 
request the Government to announce a package for the farmers who are 
indebted or adversely affected by natural calamity through waiver of loans, 
interest accrued on loans and by providing fresh loans to start agriculture 
251 

RAJYA SABHA [16 December, 2005] 
operations and such other measures  as the Government may deem 
necessary; to plug the loopholes in the procurement policy and give the 
minimum support price to the farmers wi thout any hassles; insure the farmers 
and their crops and livestock at a nominal premium or at the Government cost 
compulsorily; allocate appropriate perc entage of GDP to agriculture; make 
market intervention compulsory whe never there is bumper crop of any 
commodity; and take such other measures for the welfare of farmers as the 
Government may deem necessary. 
Sir, we find that in spite of  the support given by the State 
Governments and the Central Government, today, the farmers are, at a loss, 
because they are having small holdings and agricultural operations have 
become very costly. We find that a farmer is holding two acres of land or three 
acres of land to start cultivation a nd invest money on seeds, fertilisers, 
irrigation and electricity. When the harve st comes, the farmers are, at a loss, 
because they are not getting the minimum support price for their produce. The 
reason is, when there is a bumper crop, the intermediaries and traders get 
more profit by purchasing the farmer's produce at a distress price On the other 
hand, even when they take their produc e to the cooperative marketing area, 
or, in the State Marketing Committees, th ey take only a limited quantity, and 
the support that is being given through market intervention is not sufficient for 
the farmers. As a result, there is a lot of migration from agriculture to other 
areas. The farmers are leaving their cultivation and coming to urban areas for 
earning their livelihood. 
Sir, as per the report of the Samp le Survey Organisation, there are 
about 660 million marginal farmers. About 40 per cent of them want to leave 
cultivation because they are not .getti ng profit or even the minimum support 
price for their produce. This is the finding of the Sample Survey Organisation. 
As a result, farmers are not attracted towards agriculture. 
Sir, I am very happy that the UPA Government under Dr. Manmohan 
Singh's leadership is doing many things for the farmers. The Finance Minister 
has announced loans worth Rs.1,10,000 Crores from the nationalised banks, 
the scheduled banks and cooperative in stitutions to the farmers for the 
purpose of cultivation. Sir, I had also  put a question to the hon. Finance 
Minister that, last year, out of the to tal allocation of Rs.95,000 Crores, more 
than 80 per cent of that money was not distributed to the farmers-. This year, it 
has been increased to Rs.1.10 Crores. I told the Finance Minister to have a 
Committee at the State level and at the district level to monitor the situation, it 
should see to it that the money which has 
252 

[16 December,. 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
been earmarked for giving loan to the farmers for agricultural purposes is 
properly distributed by the various scheduled banks and the nationalised 
banks. But, unfortunately, the hon. Fi nance Minister said that he was 
reviewing it. 
Sir, as far as the nationalised banks, scheduled banks and the 
cooperative banks are concerned, they do not extend loans to the poor 
farmers. When we take the farmers to these banks, we also get negative 
replies. This is the attitude of these banks towards these poor farmers. Even a 
small and marginal farmer is mainly depending- upon the loan which is made 
available to him through the nationalised banks and the scheduled banks. 
Why are the farmers committing suicides whether it is Andhra 
Pradesh or whether it is Karnataka or whether it is Maharashtra or whether it is 
Orissa or any other State? I am not going into the politics. Farmers are 
committing suicide because of indebtedness. Indebtedness is the . major 
cause. They are not able to get t he loan from the banking institutions, 
therefore, they approach t he moneylenders, the organised gangs in the rural 
areas who charge more than four times of the interest that is generally charged 
by the banks. What happens is that the farmers are indebted and when their 
crop fails they are not able to pay back the loan and they go to the extent of 
committing suicide. Their families are in distress. This is a very serious matter. 
During last Session also, we discussed the same subject in this august House. 
With regard to the Crop Insurance Act, the State Government and the Central 
Government should take steps. Crop insurance is a solution, which will 
definitely help the farming community as  a whole. Take the case of floods, 
which are there in several parts of the country. Then, we have drought in some 
parts of the country. We find that t he farmers are at loss. When there are 
floods, the entire crop is damaged. Only a few big farmers insure their crops. 
The marginal and small farmers are not able to insure their crops. When they 
get loan from the banks sometimes they insure the crops of the farmers. Some 
of them are not doing that too. Sir, it is  high time that we took care of it. The 
hon. Prime Minister when he was the Finance Minister announced several 
times that there should be a universal insurance scheme for the farmers in this 
country. That has to be worked out because sometimes it may be a feasible 
proposition and sometimes insurance companies may not agree. But there 
should a workable solution. Chief Minister s of all the States have to be called, 
there should be a discussion, a final solution can be arrived at

RAJYA SABHA [16 December, 2005] 
as to how farmers' crops can be insured, and livestock can be insured. Today 
with a very small income the farmer has to sustain his.family. He has to 
educate his children and thereafter he has to perform functions in his family. 
With the meagre income that he is getting from the agricultural land, it is very 
difficult for him to do all these things. Therefore, Sir, the crop insurance is a 
must in order to bring them out of debt  trap as far as farmers are concerned. 
Apart from that support should be given by the Government by way of subsidy. 
Sir, earlier subsidy was being given which has been withdrawn now because 
India has entered the World Trade Organi sation as its member. There is an 
argument from all circles that on the one hand, the developed countries are
